poordeck.readme:
PoorDeck

A Stream-Deck-style control surface for your Mac — driven from your phone, tablet, or any browser on the same Wi-Fi.

PoorDeck is two projects:

  • desktop/ — a macOS menu-bar app (SwiftUI) that is the server. It hosts the client, executes the actions, holds the configuration, and gives you the editor UI for pages, buttons, and theme.
  • client/ — a Svelte + Vite web app the desktop serves. It's a thin renderer: it draws the pages and sends button presses over a WebSocket.

You install the desktop app on your Mac, then pair a device by scanning a QR code (or typing the URL). Same Wi-Fi is all it needs — no cloud, no account.

Architecture

┌──────────────── Mac ────────────────┐        ┌──── phone / tablet / web ────┐
│  PoorDeck.app (menu bar + config)    │  http  │  Svelte client                │
│  • HTTP + WebSocket server (native)  │◀──────▶│  • renders pages              │
│  • Bonjour  _poordeck._tcp           │   ws   │  • swipe to switch page       │
│  • executes actions, edits layout    │        │  • tap to fire an action      │
│  • persists layout to disk           │        │  • drives volume sliders      │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────────┘

The server is built on Network.framework — no third-party dependencies. The HTTP server serves the built client and upgrades /ws to a WebSocket that speaks the JSON protocol in desktop/…/Model/Protocol.swift (mirrored in client/src/lib/types.ts). On connect the server pushes the full resolved layout (app icons baked in as data URLs); it re-pushes whenever you edit the layout in the config window, so connected devices update live.

What it does

  • Pairing — the config window shows a QR code / URL for a device on the same network. Each device persists a stable deviceId in localStorage, so a reload or reconnect from the same phone counts as one device, not three. The config UI shows a paired badge and a live connected-device count.
  • Open / switch apps — tap a button to launch or foreground a Mac app, rendered with the app's real icon.
  • Keyboard shortcuts — post any ⌘/⌥/⌃/⇧ combo via CGEvent (needs Accessibility permission).
  • Media keys — play/pause, next, previous, fast-forward, rewind, volume up/down, mute — the standard transport keys.
  • System volume — a master-output slider + mute, live in both directions.
  • Per-app volume — Core Audio process taps drive a live list of apps playing audio: icons, horizontal sliders, per-app mute, boost up to 2×. Built on the same process-tap pipeline that powers Voulum.
  • Dock page — mirror running (and pinned) apps; tap to activate or launch.
  • Pages & orientation — swipe between pages; per-page column counts for portrait and landscape, with an optional orientation lock.
  • Editors — add/edit/delete pages and buttons and edit the theme (background, surface, text, accent, corner radius) right in the config window, with a live device preview that can follow the device's real orientation.
  • Persistence — the layout is saved as JSON in ~/Library/Application Support/PoorDeck/layout.json and reloaded on launch (seeded from a default on first run).

Run it from source

Requires Xcode, xcodegen (brew install xcodegen), and Node.

scripts/build-run.sh

That builds the client, generates + builds the app, kills any running copy, and launches the freshly built bundle (printing its version, build time, and git commit so you know it's the latest). Look for the grid icon in the menu bar; open configuration to see the QR code, then scan it from a device on the same network.

To wipe every trace of the app from your Mac — built bundles, installed copies, saved layout, and preferences:

scripts/uninstall.sh

Client dev server (hot reload)

For UI iteration you can run Vite directly, but the WebSocket needs the desktop app running to connect to:

cd client && npm run dev

Releases (DMG)

Tagged commits ship a .dmg via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/release.yml).

  • Cut a release — push a v* tag; the workflow builds a self-contained Release bundle (the client is embedded in PoorDeck.app/Contents/Resources/web), wraps it in a .dmg, and attaches it to a GitHub Release for that tag:

    git tag v0.1.0
git push origin v0.1.0

  • First release / manual run — trigger the workflow from the Actions tab ("Run workflow") and type the tag; it creates the tag's release if it doesn't exist yet.

  • Build a DMG locally — same packaging, no CI:

    scripts/make-dmg.sh          # → dist/PoorDeck-<version>.dmg

The build is ad-hoc signed only — no Apple Developer ID signature or notarization. macOS quarantines it on first launch, so open it once with right-click ▸ Open, or clear the flag:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/PoorDeck.app

pokerface.readme:
🃏 pokerface

A self-hostable, real-time planning poker app for team estimation. Paste your task links, invite the team, and vote on stories together over WebSockets. Works anonymously with no sign-up, or create an account to save sessions and keep history.

Inspired by planningpokeronline.com, kept small and hackable.

Features

  • Real-time — everyone sees votes, reveals and resets instantly over WebSockets.
  • Hidden votes — cards stay face-down until the facilitator reveals.
  • Results — average and vote distribution, with a consensus nudge.
  • Rounds from links — paste Jira / Linear / GitHub URLs (or plain lines) and each becomes a round; work through the backlog one story at a time. Add more mid-session, skip, re-activate, or set the agreed estimate when a round finishes.
  • Decks — Fibonacci and T-shirt presets, plus fully custom decks. Signed-in users get a saved default deck applied to new sessions.
  • Voting timer — the facilitator can start a 60/30/15/5s countdown per round.
  • Facilitator hand-off — the facilitator can pass the role to any participant. In an anonymous session it transfers; in an owned session the owner stays in control and the target becomes a co-facilitator (so a teammate can run the meeting).
  • Export — download any session's finished rounds and votes as CSV or a plain-text summary, from the session-complete screen or the rounds sidebar.
  • Two session modes:
    • Anonymous — pick a name, share the room URL. The session runs for 24 h, then self-destructs. The first person in runs it, and the role passes on if they leave.
    • Owned (signed in) — the session and its full vote history are saved to your account and persist indefinitely until you delete them. Only you facilitate it.
  • Accounts — optional email + password sign-in (bcrypt-hashed, JWT bearer tokens).
  • Persistent — accounts, saved sessions, rounds and vote history live in SQLite.
  • Single process — one Node server serves the API, the WebSocket, and the web app.
  • Lightweight monorepo — three small TypeScript packages, no heavy framework.

Architecture

packages/
  shared/   TypeScript types for the WebSocket protocol + REST shapes (used by both sides)
  server/   Node + ws + better-sqlite3 — REST API, live rooms, and serves the built web app
  web/      Vite + React + TypeScript client (React Router, React Query, react-hook-form)

Live room state (participants, current votes, reveal state, timer) is held in memory for speed; rooms, rounds, recorded votes and accounts are persisted to SQLite so they survive restarts. A live room is lazily loaded from the DB on first join and dropped from memory when it empties.

The web client talks to the backend over REST (/api/*) for auth and room setup, and over a WebSocket (/ws) for the live session. In dev, Vite proxies both to the server; in the all-in-one production build the server serves the built client alongside the socket.

Quick start

Requires Node 18+ and pnpm.

pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm start

Then open http://localhost:3000, create a room, and share the URL with your team. The server creates a SQLite database at ./data/pokerface.db on first run.

Set a custom port with PORT:

PORT=8080 pnpm start

Configuration

All configuration is via environment variables on the server:

Variable Default Purpose
PORT 3000 HTTP + WebSocket port.
DATABASE_PATH ./data/pokerface.db SQLite file location. Point at a persistent volume in production.
JWT_SECRET (random per boot) Signs session tokens. Set a stable value in production (see below).
ALLOWED_ORIGINS (unset = any) Comma-separated origin allowlist for the API (CORS) and WebSocket.
ALLOWED_SIGNUP_DOMAINS (unset = any) Comma-separated email-domain allowlist for registration (e.g. acme.com).

The web client has one build-time variable, VITE_WS_URL, used only for the split Railway + Vercel deploy (see below). Unset, the client talks to the same origin at /ws.

Important

If JWT_SECRET is unset, the server generates a new random secret on every boot, so every account is logged out on each restart/redeploy. If DATABASE_PATH points at a container's ephemeral disk (the default on most PaaS), accounts, saved sessions and history are wiped on every redeploy — mount a persistent volume and point DATABASE_PATH at it.

Development

Runs the server (:3000) and the Vite dev server (:5173) with hot reload:

pnpm dev

Open http://localhost:5173 during development.

Deployment (split: Railway + Vercel)

The reference deployment runs the backend on Railway and the frontend on Vercel at https://poker.oprimo.dev.

  • Backend (Railway) — deploys from railway.json. Railway builds with Nixpacks, starts @pokerface/server, and health-checks /healthz. Railway assigns a public domain like pokerface-production.up.railway.app.

  • Frontend (Vercel) — deploys from vercel.json: builds only @pokerface/web and serves packages/web/dist with an SPA rewrite. Set the build-time env var so the client knows where the backend lives:

    VITE_WS_URL = wss://<your-railway-domain>/ws

When VITE_WS_URL is unset the client falls back to the same origin, which is what the all-in-one self-host setup below relies on.

Continuous deployment

Both services auto-deploy on every push to main:

  • Railway is connected to this GitHub repo (service source → main) and rebuilds the backend on push. It needs a Volume (mounted at /data) plus the env vars DATABASE_PATH=/data/pokerface.db and JWT_SECRET so accounts and history persist. For a split deployment, also set ALLOWED_ORIGINS to your frontend origin (e.g. https://poker.oprimo.dev) so the API and WebSocket only accept requests from it.
  • Vercel is connected to the same repo and rebuilds the frontend on push, using the VITE_WS_URL project env var to reach the backend.

Self-hosting (all-in-one)

It's a single stateless Node process — deploy it anywhere that runs Node.

Docker:

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN corepack enable
COPY . .
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["pnpm", "start"]

Behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, Traefik), make sure WebSocket upgrades on /ws are forwarded. For a single instance no sticky sessions are needed; if you scale horizontally you'd need a shared room store (out of scope for this simple app).

Security

Defense is layered across the request lifecycle:

  • Origin allowlist — set ALLOWED_ORIGINS (comma-separated) to restrict both the REST API (CORS) and the WebSocket (anti-CSWSH) to those origins. Unset, any origin is accepted (convenient for the all-in-one self-host, where the app is same-origin anyway).
  • Rate limiting — register/login (20 / 15 min) and room creation (40 / hour) are capped per IP; each WebSocket connection is capped at 25 messages/second. Behind a proxy the client IP is read from X-Forwarded-For.
  • Message limits — WebSocket frames are capped at 64 KB and HTTP bodies at 1 MB.
  • Security headers — the self-hosted server sends a strict Content-Security-Policy plus X-Frame-Options: DENY (clickjacking), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy. The Vercel frontend sets the same via vercel.json.
  • Session secret — always set JWT_SECRET in production so tokens survive restarts.
  • Input guards — names, decks and pasted task text are length-clamped, and votes are validated against the active deck before they're counted.
  • By construction — all SQL is parameterized (no injection), auth is a Bearer token in a header rather than a cookie (no CSRF), passwords are bcrypt-hashed, and task URLs are restricted to http(s) so they can't become javascript: links.

Residual risk to be aware of: a room's share link is a capability URL — anyone with it can join the session and see round titles, statuses and agreed estimates. Room IDs are unguessable 10-char tokens, but treat the link like a secret. Per-person vote history is public for anonymous rooms and private to the signed-in owner for owned rooms. No user email or password data is ever exposed through the room API.

There is no email verification or password reset yet. Registration is open by default; set ALLOWED_SIGNUP_DOMAINS to your company's email domain(s) to limit who can create an account, and/or put the deployment behind your VPN/SSO.

Customizing the deck

Edit DEFAULT_DECK in packages/shared/src/index.ts.

MIT — do whatever you like.

daily-notch.readme:
DailyNotch

A macOS notch app that turns the space around your MacBook's notch into a focus timer and to-do list. Hover the notch to see today's tasks and a month of focus, start a block with one click, and watch a progress line fill up around the notch while you work.

Native SwiftUI + AppKit. macOS 14+. English and Brazilian Portuguese.

Install

  • Download: the notarized DailyNotch-X.Y.Z.dmg from Releases. Open it and drag DailyNotch to Applications. It is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it opens without warnings.
  • Mac App Store: coming soon.

The download build checks GitHub for new versions and offers them in the menu bar and in Settings > About. The App Store build updates through the store.

Features

  • Focus in the notch - the countdown and the running task sit on either side of the notch, and a progress line wraps around it and fills up as the block runs. Minimal mode shows only the line; an optional RGB line glows.
  • Hover dashboard - today's tasks (check off, start, drag to reorder, change the length inline) next to a month-long activity grid.
  • Tasks window - month calendar with dots on days that have open tasks, Day / Unscheduled lists, notes, quick add (⌘N) and per-task focus lengths.
  • Focus engine - counts down from a wall-clock deadline, so sleep and a busy Mac don't throw it off. Pauses don't count as focus time. Editing a running task's length re-bases the block.
  • Settings - a PrimoDock-style window with search: focus length, notch style, display, alerts, calendar, general, shortcuts and about.
  • Calendar - the day's events under your tasks, read-only via EventKit.
  • Global hotkey - ⌘⇧Space starts or stops focus from any app (can be switched off in Settings).
  • Multiple displays - pick the screen the notch appears on; screens without a notch get a small pill at the top center.
  • Menu bar - hourglass icon: Open Tasks, Start/Stop focus, Settings, Quit. No Dock icon until a window is open.
  • Private - no account, no analytics. Everything is saved in one JSON file in the app's sandbox container. See PRIVACY.md.

Build & run

open DailyNotch.xcodeproj   # then Cmd+R in Xcode

or from the command line:

xcodebuild -project DailyNotch.xcodeproj -scheme DailyNotch -configuration Release build

The app runs as a menu-bar / notch agent. Look for the hourglass in the menu bar, then hover your notch to open the dashboard.

Scripts

./scripts/run.sh            # build (Debug) and (re)launch
./scripts/run.sh release    # build Release and launch
./scripts/wipe.sh           # completely remove the app, data, and prefs from this Mac
./scripts/wipe.sh -y        # ... without the confirmation prompt

wipe.sh removes the built app, ~/Library/Application Support/DailyNotch, preferences, caches, and any installed copy. It does not touch this repo.

Releasing

./scripts/create-dmg.sh          # Developer ID signed + notarized build/DailyNotch-X.Y.Z.dmg
./scripts/appstore.sh            # App Store archive, exported to build/appstore
./scripts/appstore.sh --upload   # ... and uploaded to App Store Connect

create-dmg.sh reads DAILYNOTCH_SIGN_IDENTITY and DAILYNOTCH_NOTARY_PROFILE from the environment or a git-ignored .env.local. Bump MARKETING_VERSION and CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION in the Xcode project first. The App Store listing text lives in appstore/LISTING.md.

Screenshots are rendered from the app itself: the Debug build has a snapshot mode that draws every window with demo data (see DailyNotch/App/Snapshots.swift), and appstore/screenshots/compose.swift lays them out for the store (--readme for docs/images).

Hotkey

Cmd+Shift+Space - toggle the active focus session.

If the day has at least one unfinished task, the first one starts. If the day is empty, a blank session starts using the current focusMinutes setting. Press the shortcut again to stop.

The hotkey is registered via Carbon's RegisterEventHotKey (see DailyNotch/Focus/GlobalHotkey.swift), so it works from any app, not just when DailyNotch is focused.

Architecture

DailyNotch/
+- App/           NSApplication wiring, borderless notch panel, view model, focus menu state
+- Models/        Task, FocusSession, FocusSettings, Store (JSON persistence)
+- Focus/         FocusTimer (focus engine), GlobalHotkey, NotificationService
+- Notch/         Collapsed pill + expanded dashboard (to-do + activity heatmap)
+- Tasks/         Tasks window (calendar + list + add form), TaskRow, FocusTimePicker
+- Settings/      Settings window (sidebar + pages), SettingsKit, LaunchAtLoginController
+- Sync/          CalendarService (EventKit, read-only) + CalendarAuthModel
+- Design/        Theme tokens + rounded-bottom NotchShape
+- Assets.xcassets/   App icon (hourglass on black, system accent)

Key pieces:

  • NotchWindowController hangs a borderless, non-activating NSPanel from the top-center of the screen, straddling the hardware notch, and re-anchors it (top-center) as the SwiftUI content expands/collapses.
  • NotchMetrics reads the real notch width via NSScreen.auxiliaryTopLeftArea / auxiliaryTopRightArea, falling back to a synthetic pill on non-notched Macs.
  • Store is the single @MainActor source of truth, persisted to disk. Tasks sort with undone before done, then by user-controlled sortOrder, then by createdAt as a stable tiebreaker.
  • NotificationService wraps UNUserNotificationCenter and posts a single 'focus block complete' notification with the task title in the body.

Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. A few conventions to keep the project consistent:

  • Commits follow Conventional Commits: feat(scope): ..., fix(scope): ..., refactor(scope): ..., chore(scope): ..., polish(scope): ..., docs(scope): ..., ci(scope): .... Scope is the folder or layer (focus, notch, tasks, store, app, ci, etc). One logical change per commit.
  • No em-dashes or en-dashes in code, comments, commit messages, or docs. Use - (hyphen with surrounding spaces) for parenthetical asides. The same rule applies to user-facing strings shown in the app.
  • CHANGELOG is written at release time from the commit messages (cliff.toml holds the git-cliff config). You do not need to touch CHANGELOG.md in your PR.
  • Before opening a PR, run a clean Debug build locally and exercise the area you touched. The build workflow runs on every pull request and push to main; a green check is the easiest way to know it's good.
  • App icon is drawn by scripts/generate-icon.swift, which writes every size into DailyNotch/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset/. Change the script, not the PNGs.

Project file format

The .xcodeproj uses Xcode 16.3's PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup, which means the DailyNotch/ folder is auto-synced. You should rarely need to edit project.pbxproj directly - new files dropped into the folder are picked up automatically.

reviewify.readme:
Reviewify

AI reviews your pull requests. You keep the pen.

Reviewify is a self-hosted PR-review dashboard. Bring your own model key, get a full AI review in one click, then curate every comment — accept, edit, reject, or redo — before a single word reaches the PR. Run it solo or invite a team; the operator decides.

  • 🔑 Bring your own model — one OpenRouter key unlocks Claude, Kimi, Minimax, GPT and dozens more, on your quota.
  • ✋ Curate before posting — the AI proposes, a human approves. Nothing is posted to GitHub until you say so.
  • 🏠 Open & self-hostable — your diffs and keys never leave your infrastructure.
  • 📐 Standards as config — ADRs, house rules, and coding standards are first-class inputs the model actually applies.

Status: early MVP. The manual review loop (sign in → inbox → review → curate → post) is scaffolded end to end. See the roadmap.

How it works

Propose  →  Curate  →  Post
  │           │          │
  AI review   accept /   only approved
  on the      edit /     comments go
  diff        reject     to GitHub

Stack

Next.js (App Router) · PostgreSQL + Prisma · a polling worker for async reviews. Everything comes up with one docker compose up.

Quick start (self-host)

1. Register a GitHub App at https://github.com/settings/apps/new for your org or account:

  • Permissions: Pull requests (read & write), Contents (read), Metadata (read)
  • Subscribe to the Pull request webhook event
  • Callback URL: ${APP_URL}/api/auth/callback
  • Setup URL: ${APP_URL}/api/github/setup (enable "Redirect on update")
  • Webhook URL: ${APP_URL}/api/webhooks/github

2. Configure secrets:

cp .env.example .env
# generate the two secrets
openssl rand -base64 32   # -> ENCRYPTION_KEY
openssl rand -base64 32   # -> SESSION_SECRET
# then paste your GitHub App's id, client id/secret, webhook secret & private key

3. Bring it up:

docker compose up --build

Open http://localhost:3000, sign in with GitHub, install the App on your repos, and add your OpenRouter key in Settings.

Deploy to Railway

Reviewify ships with a railway.json that builds from the Dockerfile and runs migrations on boot.

  1. Create a project and add a Postgres database (Railway → New → Postgres).
  2. Deploy this repo as a service; set variables:
    • DATABASE_URL → reference the Postgres plugin (${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}})
    • ENCRYPTION_KEY, SESSION_SECRET → openssl rand -base64 32 each
    • APP_URL → your service's public URL (e.g. https://reviewify.up.railway.app)
    • GITHUB_* → from your GitHub App (paste the PEM into GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY)
  3. Add a second service from the same repo for the worker. Both services share one image; the start command dispatches on SERVICE_ROLE, so just set SERVICE_ROLE=worker on the worker service (plus the same DATABASE_URL, ENCRYPTION_KEY, and GITHUB_* variables). Leave it unset on the web service.

Point your GitHub App's callback, setup, and webhook URLs at APP_URL.

Local development

npm install
# start Postgres however you like, then point DATABASE_URL at it
npm run db:migrate       # create the schema
npm run dev              # web app on :3000
npm run worker:dev       # background review worker (separate terminal)

Run the checks CI runs:

npm run lint
npm run build
npm test                 # Vitest unit tests (diff parser, crypto)

Project layout

prisma/schema.prisma        the 8-table data model
src/lib/env.ts              validated config
src/lib/crypto.ts           AES-256-GCM for stored model keys
src/lib/providers/          OpenRouter client + the JSON findings contract
src/lib/vcs/                platform-agnostic VCS seam + GitHub impl
src/lib/review/             prompt builder + run orchestration
src/app/api/                auth, webhooks, review/finding actions
src/app/{inbox,pr,settings} the review UI
worker/                     polls for pending runs and executes them

Roadmap

  • Phase 1 — the self-hosted loop (MVP, in progress): GitHub sign-in, assigned-PR inbox, one-click review, inline curation, team rules, post to GitHub.
  • Phase 2 — depth & breadth: repo-level context beyond the diff, native Anthropic prompt caching, per-team model policy, outbound notifications.
  • Phase 3 — autopilot (gated): optional auto-review + auto-post on assignment; GitLab support.

Contributing

Issues and PRs welcome — see CONTRIBUTING.md.
